case_study_insert.main_stem: Terrace Grove Beverages (TGB) is a private limited company in the craft soft-drink sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2012 by Priya Raval, it bottles sparkling fruit drinks for regional supermarkets and health-food chains and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TGB plans to invest $720,000 in a new automated bottling line with recyclable glass bottles, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.80 a unit and a selling price of $9.30, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. TGB faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8%, labour turnover is rising, and waste on the bottling line has reached 6%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q2 2025: The sparkling-drink line filled 18,000 bottles last month at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 2.8 days. A survey of 450 shoppers found that 61% would pay up to $0.35 more for recyclable bottles, and 48% check packaging before buying. A skills audit shows 14 of 52 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new filler; off-the-job training at the local college costs $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Terrace Grove Beverages as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (October 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs on TGB's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.50 to $14.28 per hour from April 2026, lifting TGB's wage bill. (3) Wholesale sugar, juice and glass input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on sparkling drinks grew 2.9%.

questions.question_text: TGB plans to finance part of its bottling-line expansion with a $420,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TGB of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs TGB nothing in interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the firm already carries a $420,000 bank loan and has committed $720,000 to the new bottling line. Every dollar not paid as interest can instead absorb the 9.6% rise in juice, sugar and glass input costs, helping TGB hold its $9.30 selling price for regional supermarkets rather than passing costs on and risking lost shelf space.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk attached to a bank loan, so the $300,000 is available without putting TGB's recyclable-glass bottling line at risk of repossession if demand for sparkling drinks falls short of the 80,000-unit plan. It also preserves founder Priya Raval's ownership and control: no lender can impose conditions on how the flat, democratic team runs the filler or allocates the $180,000 a year of fixed costs. Retained profit is therefore the cheaper and lower-risk source for this particular expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to TGB's costs, expansion and financing mix.

questions.question_text: TGB is launching a new recyclable-bottle sparkling drink. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TGB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A national TV campaign would build brand awareness for the new recyclable-bottle sparkling drink across all the regional supermarkets and health-food chains that stock TGB, reaching millions of viewers quickly. However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 52-employee business that has just committed $720,000 to a bottling line, and much of the national audience lies outside TGB's regional distribution, so a large share of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper than television and reaches TGB's core regional catchment with time-sensitive launch messages, fitting the 2.8-day order-fulfilment story and the 18,000-bottle monthly volume. Its weakness is narrow reach: TGB also supplies health-food chains beyond the local area, so radio alone cannot generate the 80,000-unit volume needed to justify the new filler.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can target exactly the 61% of 450 surveyed shoppers who would pay up to $0.35 more for recyclable bottles and the 48% who check packaging before buying. Engagement is measurable, cost per reached shopper is low, and the recyclable-glass story can be shown directly to health-conscious buyers nationally. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but the segment fit is strongest.

Recommendation: TGB should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise research-identified segment, costs far less than national television, and scales nationally unlike local radio, while reinforcing the recyclable-bottle positioning that supports the $9.30 selling price. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 52-staff firm funding a $720,000 expansion; radio is rejected as too narrow for its widening distribution. TGB should add modest in-store supermarket displays to convert the interest the influencers generate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to TGB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in TGB's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in TGB's context and recommends influencer marketing with clear reasons for rejecting television and radio.

questions.question_text: TGB's absenteeism has reached 8% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for TGB of using democratic leadership to improve motivation on the bottling line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives TGB's 52 employees a real voice in how the new bottling line is organised, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help set filler routines and shift patterns are more likely to attend consistently, directly reducing the 8% absenteeism rate and easing pressure on the flat structure without adding supervisors.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions also draws on the practical knowledge of the people who handle the filler every day, generating ideas that can cut the 6% bottling-line waste and protect the 2.4% defect rate. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, avoiding further $750-per-employee off-the-job training costs at the local college and protecting output of 80,000 units while the $720,000 line beds in. Democratic leadership therefore tackles both motivation and quality at low cost.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development linked to TGB's absenteeism, waste, training costs and output.

questions.question_text: TGB must upskill 14 production staff to operate the new filler. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should TGB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the filler is directly relevant to TGB's own machines and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 14 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 18,000-bottle monthly output and the improvement to a 2.4% defect rate. Drawbacks are that the trainers are production staff whose own work suffers, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no external certificate, which may matter if supermarket chains demand formal records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $750 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 14 staff, costing $10,500 in total — modest beside the $720,000 investment. It removes staff from the line, however, reducing short-term capacity when absenteeism is already 8%, and generic content may not match TGB's exact filler settings, so follow-up coaching on site would still be needed.

Decision: TGB should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, backed by short college sessions for the most senior operators. On-the-job training is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids further output loss while 8% absenteeism already strains the line; full off-the-job training is rejected because spending $10,500 and withdrawing 14 staff would disrupt the supermarket delivery schedule, and TGB can add college visits later once the new filler stabilises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited application to TGB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in TGB's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in TGB's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TGB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety versus 80,000-unit output; discount modelling against $180,000 fixed costs; loan-service feasibility for the $720,000 line; and unit-cost benchmarking at $7.05 to tackle 6% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate answer in each calculation; 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($9.30 − $4.80) = $180,000 ÷ $4.50 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.30 − $4.80 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TGB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 40,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 80,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 40,000 units, to judge whether the new $720,000 bottling line can be run near full capacity.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.50 lets managers model a supermarket discount: a $0.30 cut would reduce contribution to $4.20, showing how much extra volume is needed to cover $180,000 of fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $180,000 and contribution helps set the sales volume required to service the $420,000 bank loan, so the board can test repayment feasibility before authorising more capital.
4. Unit cost of $7.05 ($180,000 ÷ 80,000 units + $4.80) lets TGB benchmark each quarter and pinpoint the 6% bottling-line waste, supporting negotiations over the 9.6% input-cost rises.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TGB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TGB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.20 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.40 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.06 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $70,000 inventories + $125,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $240,000; 2025 current assets = $68,000 + $150,000 + $62,000 = $280,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $200,000 in both years gives 1.20 and 1.40. Excluding inventories, $170,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.85 in 2024 and $212,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.06 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The ratio covering all current assets rose from 1.20 to 1.40 as current assets grew from $240,000 to $280,000 while current liabilities held at $200,000. The stricter measure, which strips out inventories, improved from 0.85 to 1.06, so TGB now covers short-term debts without relying on selling stock — important while it services a $420,000 bank loan and funds a $720,000 expansion. However, trade receivables climbed from $125,000 to $150,000, tying up cash; if supermarket and health-food customers pay late, the stronger position could deteriorate quickly, and inventories edged down to $68,000, so stock availability for peak demand should be watched.

Conclusion: TGB's financial position has improved. Both measures show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The residual risk is rising receivables, so TGB should tighten credit control while proceeding with the bottling-line investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates both ratios for both years accurately with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TGB of using recyclable bottles for its sparkling-drink range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recyclable bottles match the preferences of the 61% of 450 surveyed shoppers who would pay up to $0.35 more, allowing TGB to protect the $4.50 contribution per unit as the 9.6% rise in sugar, juice and glass input costs bites. The 48% who check packaging before buying also strengthen TGB's brand with health-food chains, helping it retain listings for the $720,000 bottling line.

Disadvantage: Recyclable glass typically costs more than conventional plastic, which would push up the $4.80 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $0.35 premium is accepted. Heavier or more fragile bottles could also raise the current 6% bottling-line waste and the 2.4% defect rate through breakage before the new filler stabilises, offsetting the marketing gain.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using TGB's research, costs and waste data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in input costs will affect TGB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If TGB's $420,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 × $420,000). That is small beside $180,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan were fixed-rate the effect would be zero. Higher rates may make consumers more cautious about premium sparkling drinks and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but TGB can largely cap this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.28 per hour): TGB employs a workforce of 52 in bottling and packing roles, so this rise feeds directly into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no total wage bill can be honestly invented; the sound judgement is against the given productivity data — 80,000 units ÷ 52 staff is about 1,538 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $4.50 contribution.

Input cost inflation (9.6% sugar, juice and glass): The insert never decomposes the $4.80 variable cost, so only a bound is defensible — if the whole variable cost rose 9.6% it would add 9.6% × $4.80 = $0.46 per unit, and at 80,000 units that is about $36,800 a year. Even a smaller pass-through would cut contribution below $4.50. TGB can recover part through the $0.35 recyclable-bottle premium and supermarket price talks, but the effect repeats on every bottle.

Conclusion: The 9.6% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 80,000 units, directly erodes the $4.50 contribution that justifies the $720,000 line, and cannot be neutralised by fixing a loan rate as the interest risk can. The wage rise is significant but manageable through productivity; the interest rise is the smallest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to TGB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on TGB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in context with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
